prompt: An attacker copies the account table. Match each way of storing passwords to what the attacker can do.

pairs.match: Recover every password if they also get the key
Only test guesses against each record; the passwords themselves aren't there

explanation: The login system needs to verify a password without keeping a recoverable copy.

prompt: Match each operation to its example use.

pairs.match: Protecting a stored document that must be recovered later
Checking a submitted password at login

explanation: Password hashing is a salted, deliberately costly calculation that produces a verifier.

prompt: Order the steps of checking a password at login.
steps: Retrieve the saved hash, salt and settings
Hash the submitted password using that saved salt and those settings
Compare the result with the saved hash
explanation: This is verification. It does not decrypt or recover the original password.

prompt: Order the steps of saving a new password.
steps: The student submits a chosen password over HTTPS
The password-hashing library generates a random salt
The library computes the hash with its configured cost
The application stores the hash, salt and settings
explanation: The original password is not saved in the account table or logs.

prompt: Adding a salt to SHA-256 gives the same protection as Argon2id.
explanation: A salt stops equality and shared-precomputation shortcuts but does not add Argon2id's memory and time cost. Do not build a homemade loop around a general-purpose hash.

prompt: Even with a unique salt on every record, an attacker who copies the password database can still test guesses such as "blue" against each record.
explanation: The attacker normally gets the salts too. Salts prevent matching equal values and precomputation shortcuts; cost settings make each guess expensive; strong unique passwords still matter.

prompt: In an old breach, thousands of accounts had exactly the same stored encrypted password value. What does that reveal, and what would have prevented it?

options.text: They share a password; a unique salt per record would have hidden that
The encryption key leaked; a longer key would have prevented it
options.why: Identical values point to identical passwords, not a leaked key.

options.text: Nothing; identical values are a random coincidence at that scale
options.why: Thousands of identical values aren't coincidence; they're the same password.

options.text: The passwords must be strong, since they all encrypt to one value
options.why: Identical values mean many users chose the same, probably weak, password.

explanation: Cracking one would crack them all. Salts prevent equality and precomputation shortcuts, but do not make a weak password strong.

prompt: Why are stored password hints a problem, even if the passwords themselves are protected?

options.text: Readable hints narrow down what the password might be
Hints make the password-hashing step noticeably slower
options.why: Hints don't affect hashing speed; they reveal clues to the password.

options.text: Hints are encrypted with the same key, so they leak it
options.why: Hints are usually stored readable; the problem is what they say.

options.text: Hints are only a problem when longer than the password
options.why: Even short hints like a pet's name give attackers a head start.

explanation: Changing the encryption algorithm does not fix what readable hints disclose. Provide a proper reset flow instead of keeping a clue to the existing password.

prompt: The Base64 encoding of the salt and hash in an Argon2id record is a form of encryption.
explanation: Base64 represents binary data as text. It is encoding, not encryption.

prompt: Why is an IP address not reliable evidence of who is making a request?

options.text: Addresses are shared and can change over time
HTTPS encrypts IP addresses so servers can't read them
options.why: Servers do see IP addresses; HTTPS doesn't hide them.

options.text: Browsers hide the user's IP address from every server
options.why: Browsers don't hide the client's IP address from servers.

options.text: IP addresses are only used for email, not web requests
options.why: IP addresses are used for all internet traffic, including web requests.

explanation: Many users behind one NAT gateway or proxy share an address, and a phone moving from Wi-Fi to mobile data changes address mid-visit. Cookies and sessions provide the context for later requests.

prompt: Complete the definitions.
text: Authentication checks [[evidence for a claimed identity|whether an action is permitted|that input is well formed]]. Authorisation checks [[whether a particular action is permitted|evidence for a claimed identity|that the session cookie is Secure]].
explanation: A student may read their own results; a lecturer may enter marks for an assigned module. Login alone does not grant either.

prompt: Which parts are stored in a password-hash record such as an Argon2id string? Select all that apply.

options.text: The algorithm name
The salt
The hash
The cost settings
The original password
options.why: The original password is never stored; that's the point of hashing.

options.text: An encryption key for the password
options.why: There's no key to recover the password; the record is verified, not decrypted.

explanation: Everything needed to repeat the calculation is stored. Nothing in the record is the original password or a key to recover it.

prompt: At login, a developer generates a fresh salt, hashes the submitted password with it, and compares the result with the stored hash. What is wrong?

options.text: It must reuse the stored salt, so it will never match
Nothing: using a fresh salt at every login is more secure
options.why: A fresh salt gives a different result, so the right password would never match.

options.text: It should decrypt the stored hash and compare plain text
options.why: Password hashes can't be decrypted; you repeat the calculation instead.

options.text: It should compare the two salts instead of the two hashes
options.why: Salts are stored values; comparing them doesn't check the password.

explanation: Use the password library's verify function. It reads the salt and settings from the stored record, repeats the calculation and compares the results.

prompt: What is the difference between a password library's verify function and Argon2id?

options.text: Verify is the library call that checks a password; Argon2id is the algorithm it uses
They are just two different names for the same hashing algorithm
options.why: One is a library function and the other is the algorithm it calls.

options.text: Argon2id is the library call; verify is the algorithm it runs
options.why: This swaps them: the library function calls the Argon2id algorithm.

options.text: Verify decrypts the stored Argon2id record to read the password
options.why: Nothing is decrypted; the function repeats the hash and compares.

explanation: A match lets authentication proceed, subject to account status and any extra factor. It does not authorise access to every record.

prompt: A student logs in to a results website, then opens their results page. Match each step to the question the server must answer.

pairs.match: Has the student proved they own this account, for example with the right password?
Does this request carry a valid session?
May this account read these results?

explanation: Verify the password, keep a session, check permission.

prompt: HTTPS and password hashing each protect what?

options.text: HTTPS protects the password in transit; hashing protects it once stored
HTTPS protects it in storage; hashing protects it in transit
options.why: This swaps them: HTTPS covers transit and hashing covers storage.

options.text: Both of them only protect the password while it is being sent
options.why: Hashing protects the stored record, not the password in transit.

options.text: Using HTTPS makes password hashing unnecessary on the server
options.why: HTTPS doesn't protect the stored database if it's stolen.

explanation: They address different moments in the password's life.

prompt: Argon2id is configured to use a large amount of working memory for each calculation. Does each stored password record take up that much space?

options.text: No: the memory is only used while the hash is being worked out
Yes: each record stores the full working memory alongside it
options.why: Records only store the algorithm, settings, salt and hash, which is a short string.

options.text: Only the salt is that large; the rest of the record is quite small
options.why: Salts are short random values, not large blocks of memory.

options.text: Only administrator accounts use that much storage per record
options.why: Every account's record is the same size whatever its role.

explanation: The server pays the memory cost during every verification, which is why concurrent logins need benchmarking and limits on work in flight.

prompt: Why is a fast hash such as SHA-256 a poor choice for storing passwords?

options.text: It makes each guess fast and cheap for an attacker
It can be decrypted by anyone who has the right key
options.why: Hashes can't be decrypted; the problem is guessing is fast.

options.text: It gives different output each time for the same input
options.why: A hash gives the same output for the same input; that's how verification works.

options.text: It can't handle long passwords or special characters
options.why: SHA-256 handles long inputs fine; the problem is its speed.

explanation: SHA-256 is designed to be fast, which suits integrity checks. Argon2id deliberately makes each guess cost time and memory.

prompt: What does Argon2id's memory cost do to an attacker with a stolen password database?

options.text: Each guess costs memory and time, so guessing at large scale becomes expensive
It stops the attacker from being able to make any guesses at all
options.why: Attackers can still make guesses; each one just costs more.

options.text: It encrypts the stolen database so the attacker can't read it
options.why: Argon2id doesn't encrypt the database; it makes each guess expensive.

options.text: It only slows down the legitimate server, not the attacker
options.why: The cost applies to every guess, including the attacker's.

explanation: Slower guessing buys protection, but a predictable password can still be found. The server also pays this cost, so benchmark concurrent logins.

prompt: Why must the stored password record include the algorithm, salt and cost settings?

options.text: Checking a password has to repeat exactly the same calculation
So the original password can be recovered if it's forgotten
options.why: Hash records can't be reversed; recovery needs a reset flow.

options.text: So users can view their own security settings in their profile
options.why: The settings are for verification, not for users to view.

options.text: To make the record longer and harder for attackers to read
options.why: Length doesn't protect anything; the settings let the check be repeated.

explanation: The library reuses the recorded salt and settings, then compares the result with the stored hash.

prompt: Argon2id makes each password guess slower and more costly, but weak passwords can still be guessed.
explanation: It makes each guess more expensive. Strong, unique passwords still matter.

prompt: What is the random value generated for each password record so that identical passwords produce different stored hashes?
explanation: The salt is stored with the hash. It prevents equality and precomputation shortcuts but does not strengthen a weak password.

prompt: A site raises its Argon2id memory cost for new hashes. What happens to existing users' stored records?

options.text: Each is re-hashed with the new settings at that user's next successful login
Every existing user must reset their password before they can log in again
options.why: Each record stores its own settings, so old records still verify.

options.text: The server decrypts every stored record overnight and hashes it again
options.why: Hash records can't be decrypted; the password is only available when the user logs in.

options.text: Old records stop verifying, because the configured settings have changed
options.why: Verification uses the settings saved in each record, not the current configuration.

explanation: Because every record stores its own settings, old records still verify. After a successful login the server holds the correct password, so it can hash it again with the new settings and save the upgraded record.
